cards.explanation: The answer is eight years old. Josiah, king of Judah, takes the throne at eight and reigns in Jerusalem thirty-one years. I can't stick with a gym membership for thirty-one days, friends. This boy stuck with a kingdom.

The answer is that he does what's right in the LORD's eyes. Josiah did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in the ways of his father David. The text adds that he did not turn aside to the right or to the left. A straight line, friends, and I can't even cut one through a cookie sheet.

The answer is True. In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still young, Josiah began to seek the God of his father David. Josiah, king of Judah, was young, and he began seeking God. That's a good place to start, friends.

The answer is the high places and idols. In his twelfth year Josiah began to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images. That's a long list, and he works through it. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer and never cleared out a single thing.

The answer is False. The text says the altars of the Baals were torn down in his presence. Josiah, king of Judah, was there when it happened. So staying back at the palace doesn't fit what the verse says.

The answer is graves. Josiah shattered the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images, crushed them to dust, and scattered them over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. It's a heavy moment, so I'll just leave it right there.

The answer is False. After Judah and Jerusalem were cleansed, Josiah did the same in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali, and in the ruins around them. This job had a long list, and he kept on until the work was done.
The answer is back to Jerusalem. After tearing down the altars and Asherah poles throughout the land of Israel, the text says he returned to Jerusalem. That's the city where he reigned.

The answer is to repair the house of the LORD. Josiah sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the LORD his God. The text says this was in order to cleanse the land and the temple. Three men, one big repair job.

The answer is False. The Levites who guarded the doors collected the money from the people of Manasseh and Ephraim, from all the remnant of Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from the people of Jerusalem. Jerusalem was just one of the groups. That's a lot of folks giving to one house.

The answer is those supervising the work. The three men gave the money to Hilkiah the high priest, and then it was put into the hands of those supervising the work in the house of the LORD. They in turn gave it to the workmen restoring and repairing the house. The money moves down the line to where the work is.

The answer is dressed stone. The text says they gave money to the carpenters and builders to buy dressed stone, as well as timbers for couplings and beams for the buildings. That's solid building material for a worn-down house. Repairs aren't glamorous, friends, but I love them.
The answer is True. The text says plainly, "And the men did the work faithfully." That's a good thing to have said about you. I'd settle for "the cookies came out even."

The answer is task by task. The text says the Levites over the laborers supervised all who did the work, task by task. That's steady attention, not a drive-by. It's like checking each tray as it goes in, and I only learned that after a few sad batches.
The answer is secretaries and gatekeepers. The text says some of the Levites were secretaries, officers, and gatekeepers. Some of the Levites held jobs like these, and the text names them.
